input.content:
# Whodunit working brief

Whodunit finds the commit that broke an AI agent. It shows what that commit was asked to do, fixes it, proves the fix, and reports what the breakage cost. The pitch in one line: "41 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?"

This is the brief for whoever writes code here, human or coding agent. Read it before changing anything.

## Sessions in this repo are published

Entire records every coding session in this repo and the repo is public, so the whole transcript of a session can be read by anyone. Treat everything typed, read or printed during a session as public.

- Keys live in `.env`, which git ignores. Never print a value from it, never paste one into a prompt, and never open it with a tool that echoes its contents. Load it inside the code that needs it.
- Do not open private notes, mail, chat logs or any file outside this repo from a session here. If the work seems to need one, stop and ask the owner.
- Email and phone redaction is switched on in `.entire/settings.json`. After the first commit, read the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain --transcript` before anything is pushed.
- Never run `entire enable` with `--import-history`. It would pull older sessions from this folder into the public record.

## How one case runs

1. Read neatlogs and neatroots to get the failing runs and the time the failures began.
2. List the suspect commits between the last good ref and the first bad one.
3. Replay the failing inputs against suspect commits in git worktrees. Agent failures are random, so repeat until the result is statistically confident.
4. Name the culprit and pull the Entire checkpoint behind it, which holds the original request and the session.
5. Ask the owner one question (revert, or keep the intent and patch) and remember the ruling.
6. Fix, replay to prove the fix, add the case as a permanent regression test, and open a PR or an Entire Trail.
7. Write the damage (bad runs and dollars) to cfo.ai.

Any description of the project opens with "which commit, and why". The fix comes after that.

## Layout

Python 3.12 through uv, in one repo.

- `whodunit/case.py`: a case is a symptom, the failing inputs, a good ref, a bad ref and a check.
- `whodunit/suspects.py`: the commits in `good..bad` with their Entire checkpoint ids. Commits that cannot reach the agent's code get a lower prior (path filter first, then entire-graph impact).
- `whodunit/replay.py`: one git worktree per commit under test. It runs the target's replay command with the case input, tags the run with the commit SHA and case id, and reads the verdict from neatroots findings or a local check. A commit that will not build is skipped, like `git bisect skip`.
- `whodunit/lineup.py`: the statistical bisect, described below.
- `whodunit/motive.py`: `entire checkpoint explain` and `entire why` for the culprit, which give the original request and the session.
- `whodunit/brief.py`: the model writes the root-cause brief from the culprit diff, the relevant slice of the session transcript and a diff of a failing run against a passing one. Every sentence cites a span id, a commit or a checkpoint.
- `whodunit/ruling.py`: the ask-once memory (revert or patch, per kind of change), stored as files in the repo and mirrored to Entire Brain.
- `whodunit/fix.py`: applies the fix on a branch, replays the case until the posterior says it is fixed, adds the case to `cases/` as a regression test, and opens the PR or Trail.
- `whodunit/damages.py`: counts bad runs and cost from traces and writes them to cfo.ai.
- `whodunit/casefile/`: the static HTML case file, which is the main demo surface, and the CLI command `whodunit open-case`.
- `victims/refund-agent/`: the demo target. It starts from the refund agent in neatroots' `examples/` (Apache-2.0, and the README must say so) and grows to 40 or more commits through real coding-agent requests in a separate session, so the history and its checkpoints are genuine.

### The statistical bisect

Model a single change point c. The failure rate is p_good before c and p_bad from c onward. Estimate both rates by running the two endpoints several times and keeping Beta posteriors. Hold a posterior over c. Each round, test the commit that splits the posterior mass most evenly and update with the Bernoulli outcome. Stop at 95% on one commit or when the replay budget runs out, and in the second case report the remaining suspects with their probabilities.

Unit-test it against a simulator. Publish the curve of accuracy against replay budget, next to plain bisect, at failure rates from 100% down to 20%.

## Tool facts checked on 10 October 2026

### neatroots

Version 0.2.6 is installed at `~/.local/bin/neatroots` and serves on port 4100. It is a local collector with checks and replay, and its MCP endpoint is `http://localhost:4100/mcp`.

- Whole-agent replay: `neatroots rerun add <project> "<command>" --cwd <dir>`, then `neatroots replay <trace-id> [--input ...]`. The agent receives `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_INPUT`, `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_ID` and `NEATLOGS_ENDPOINT`.
- Checks are YAML files in `.neatroots/checks/`. The `rule` kinds (repeat, errors, count, threshold, match, run_end) need no model. `yes_no` questions return a probability and need neatroots' local model, which is not installed on this machine, so use rule checks.
- `neatroots mock-llm` is a key-free stand-in LLM on port 4110.
- `neatroots status` reports "cloud no key", so importing cloud traces needs the project key configured first.
- MCP tools used here: `search_runs`, `get_run_outline`, `list_findings`, `compare_runs`, `rerun`, `replay`, `query_sql`, `import_cloud_trace`.

### neatlogs cloud

The MCP endpoint is `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/mcp` with the project key as a Bearer token. `search_traces` does full-text search over names, errors and metadata, and no tag filter is documented, so check early that a commit SHA stored in metadata can be searched. `get_trace_context` returns the span tree with inputs and outputs. `get_detection_trend` returns hour or day buckets and dates the onset of failures. The Python SDK needs Python 3.10 to 3.13, takes the Project API key (the `nlw_` key returns 401), and needs `neatlogs.flush()` before exit. `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` checks the setup.

### Entire

CLI 0.11.4. It captures a checkpoint when a commit follows agent work, stores it under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, and adds an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer to the commit.

- `entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --json` returns metadata, and `--transcript` returns the session JSONL.
- `entire why FILE:LINE --json` returns the commit, checkpoint, prompt and session behind a line. `entire blame` works per file.
- `entire plugin install graph`, then `entire graph init-agents --repo .`, sets up entire-graph. Brain is `entire brain setup`. Trails need `entire runner setup -y`.
- Checkpoint links take the form `https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/FULL_SHA`.
- Not yet verified: whether the hooks fire for sessions run in the desktop app. Run `entire checkpoint list` after the first commit. If it is empty, run the coding agent from a terminal.

### cfo.ai

The MCP endpoint is `https://api.cfo.ai/mcp` and uses OAuth, which the owner has to authorise. Tools include `edit_table_blocks`, `edit_scenarios` and `edit_pages`. The plan should be a multi-page model with stated assumptions, upside and downside scenarios, and a simulator. Every write to cfo.ai needs the owner's yes.

## Models and spend

- Replays of the refund agent use the small Haiku model on the hackathon gateway (OpenAI-compatible, `LITELLM_BASE_URL` and `LITELLM_API_KEY` in `.env`, $20 budget). Three parallel calls on 10 October each returned in about 1.4 seconds with no throttling. The owner's own API key is the fallback and should be a one-setting switch.
- Most development runs should use `neatroots mock-llm` or a scripted fake LLM and cost nothing.
- Never change model or provider inside one case. The bisect compares failure rates across commits, and a model change would look like a regression.
- Investigation and fix run through the coding agent in headless mode. The repo must also work with a plain API key so other people can run it. Keep `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` out of the shell that launches the coding agent, and load `.env` only inside the replay code.
- Grading starts with neatroots rule checks, which use no model. The bisect itself uses no model.
- Keep investigations to about 10 before Sunday 11 October, 4:30 PM IST, and run the full eval after that.

## AWS

There is one shared $25 allowance and nothing meters it, so stop resources when they are idle. Use us-east-1 only, the pre-provisioned `Hackathon_VPC`, instance types t2, t3 or t3a from nano to large, and volumes of 50 GB or less. Only one EC2 instance may exist at a time, so terminate before replacing. Bedrock is not included. - Email and phone redaction is switched on in `.entire/settings.json`. After the first commit, read the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain --transcript` before anything is pushed.

- `whodunit/lineup.py`: the statistical bisect, described below.
- `whodunit/motive.py`: `entire checkpoint explain` and `entire why` for the culprit, which give the original request and the session.

1. Saturday 10 PM: repo up, Entire on with the first checkpoint verified, neatlogs and neatroots receiving runs, the victim agent running, first #neatHack post.
2. Sunday 3 AM: replay runner over worktrees. Plain bisect finds an always-failing planted bug across 20 commits.
3. Sunday 10 AM: the statistical bisect finds a bug that fails about 30% of the time, and the simulator chart is done. This milestone matters most.
4. Sunday 6 PM: motive, brief, ruling memory, fix and verify, case file page v1.
5. Monday 2 AM: sealed-key eval on the grown victim, neatlogs cloud link (the detection trend dates the onset), cfo.ai model through MCP, parallel replays on the AWS allowance.
6. Monday noon: stretch target, README, evidence folder.
7. Monday 6 PM: demo video, which opens on "41 commits, which one did it?" and names the culprit inside 30 seconds. Submit at 7 PM.

If milestone 3 slips past Sunday 2 PM, drop the stretch target and the AWS runner and keep everything else.

## Case file design

This direction is a proposal and the owner has not signed it off yet.

The metaphor is a detective's typed case file with a two-colour typewriter ribbon.

- Light: paper `#F3EDDF`, surface `#E9E0CC`, ink `#201B15`, muted ink `#6B6156`, rule `#D8CDB6`, and one accent, ribbon red `#B4261F`.
- Dark: background `#1B1714`, surface `#26201A`, ink `#EDE4D3`, accent `#E5604F`.
- Type from Google Fonts: Young Serif for titles, Alegreya Sans for interface text, Courier Prime for typed evidence.
- Scale 13, 15, 17, 21, 27, 34, 44, 58 px. Line heights 1.1 for display, 1.2 for headings, 1.55 for body, 1.45 for Courier.
- Sample copy: "Suspects: 41. Cleared: 40." / "Motive: someone asked for friendlier replies." / "Alibi: never touched the agent." / empty state "No cases yet. Lucky you." / button "Open a case".

It should feel like a well-made object. That rules out pure white backgrounds, purple or blue gradients, glass effects, Inter as the only typeface, the three-card feature grid, sparkle icons, icons in rounded squares, fake KPI dashboards, stock hero sections and decorative emoji.

## Writing rules

These cover UI copy, the README, the pitch, scripts, commit messages and code comments.

- The voice is a kind, witty human. No "Supercharge", "Unlock", "Seamlessly" or "AI-powered".
- No em or en dashes, no "not X but Y" constructions, no one-line closers, no forced groups of three, no bold-label lists. Headings use sentence case.
- Repo text says "the coding agent" and names no assistant or vendor.
- Be specific: names, numbers, real copy.

## Working rules

- Commits carry no co-author trailer.
- These need the owner's yes each time: the first push to GitHub, any post on X, a PR or comment on someone else's repo, any write to cfo.ai, and launching anything on AWS.
- The owner does browser signups and enters any card or password personally.
- Report failures as plainly as successes. The eval is only worth something if the misses are in it.

1	# Whodunit
2	
3	41 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?
4	
5	Whodunit answers two questions about an AI agent that used to work and now fails: which commit broke it, and why that commit was made. Then it fixes the commit, proves the fix by replaying the failures, and counts what the breakage cost.
6	
7	It was built for neatHack between 10 and 12 October 2026. `hackathon.md` is the dated build log, including the parts that went wrong.
8	
9	## Why plain bisect is not enough
10	
11	`git bisect` assumes a bad commit fails every time. Agents do not behave that way. A prompt change might break one run in three, and a commit that is perfectly fine might still fail one run in twenty. Test a bad commit once, see it pass, and bisect walks off in the wrong direction without telling you.
12	
13	Whodunit replays the failing inputs against suspect commits and keeps a probability for each suspect being the first bad one. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure. If the replay budget runs out first, it hands back the suspects still in the lineup with their probabilities.
14	
15	How well that works is measured two ways. [eval/sealed](eval/sealed/README.md) is five regressions planted by a separate session with a sealed answer key: three were named inside 120 replays, all five after more, and no commit was wrongly accused. [eval/simulator](eval/simulator/README.md) is simulated cases with a known culprit. The short version: when good commits never fail, plain bisect with repeats is cheaper. When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own, it falls apart and the statistical bisect does not.
16	
17	## How a case runs
18	
19	A case is a small TOML file: a symptom, the failing inputs with what each should have produced, the last good ref and the first bad ref. One command runs all of it:
20	
21	```bash
22	uv run whodunit investigate cases/whole-history.toml --from-traffic refund-agent
23	```
24	
25	It stops only when it needs the owner's ruling. Each step is also a command of its own (`lineup`, `brief`, `ruling`, `fix`, `damages`, `open-case`), and each adds to one record next to the case file. The case file page is drawn from that record.
26	
27	On the refund agent's real history, 57 commits grown by a separate coding session, that command named the culprit at 99.8% after 20 replays, quoted the request that caused it, patched it, proved the patch on 30 clean replays and counted 120.00 in refunds that had gone to the wrong people. [evidence/casefile-whole-history.png](evidence/casefile-whole-history.png) is the page it wrote.
28

And ordinary runs that already asked what the case asks are evidence that is already paid for.
30	1. The lineup checks every suspect commit out into its own git worktree and replays the case inputs there. Each replay is a real run of the agent, traced to neatroots and tagged with the commit and the case. A commit that will not build is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does.
31	2. The motive comes from Entire. A commit made by a coding agent carries a checkpoint, and the checkpoint holds the session. Whodunit finds the prompt that led to the commit and what the coding agent did next.
32	3. The brief is written by a model from the culprit's diff, that slice of the session, and a failing run set against a passing one. Every sentence has to cite a span, a commit or a checkpoint that is really in the evidence. Sentences that do not are cut.
33	4. The ruling is the owner's. It is asked once per kind of change (a prompt change, a tool change, a dependency) and remembered under `rulings/`.
34	5. The fix is a revert or a patch on a local branch. It is proven only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%, which takes about 30 clean replays. A patch that is not proven is tried once more with its failures in view, and after that the culprit is reverted. The case is kept under `cases/` as a regression test that `whodunit check` can replay against any ref.
35	6. The damages are counted from the traces: how many runs went bad since the culprit, what they cost in tokens, and what they cost the shop, read from the refund tool's spans.
36	
37	Whodunit never pushes, opens a pull request or writes to anyone's finance model by itself. Those stay with the owner.
38	
39	## Try it

42

45	uv run pytest -m "not slow"                    # the fast tests, no model and no keys

48	uv run python tests/planted.py /tmp/planted

54

# Whodunit

41 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?

Whodunit answers two questions about an AI agent that used to work and now fails: which commit broke it, and why that commit was made. Then it fixes the commit, proves the fix by replaying the failures, and counts what the breakage cost.

It was built for neatHack between 10 and 12 October 2026. `hackathon.md` is the dated build log, including the parts that went wrong.

## Why plain bisect is not enough

`git bisect` assumes a bad commit fails every time. Agents do not behave that way. A prompt change might break one run in three, and a commit that is perfectly fine might still fail one run in twenty. Test a bad commit once, see it pass, and bisect walks off in the wrong direction without telling you.

Whodunit replays the failing inputs against suspect commits and keeps a probability for each suspect being the first bad one. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure. If the replay budget runs out first, it hands back the suspects still in the lineup with their probabilities.

How well that works is measured two ways. [eval/sealed](eval/sealed/README.md) is five regressions planted by a separate session with a sealed answer key: three were named inside 120 replays, all five after more, and no commit was wrongly accused. [eval/simulator](eval/simulator/README.md) is simulated cases with a known culprit. The short version: when good commits never fail, plain bisect with repeats is cheaper. When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own, it falls apart and the statistical bisect does not.

## How a case runs

A case is a small TOML file: a symptom, the failing inputs with what each should have produced, the last good ref and the first bad ref. One command runs all of it:

```bash
uv run whodunit investigate cases/whole-history.toml --from-traffic refund-agent
```

It stops only when it needs the owner's ruling. Each step is also a command of its own (`lineup`, `brief`, `ruling`, `fix`, `damages`, `open-case`), and each adds to one record next to the case file. The case file page is drawn from that record.

On the refund agent's real history, 57 commits grown by a separate coding session, that command named the culprit at 99.8% after 20 replays, quoted the request that caused it, patched it, proved the patch on 30 clean replays and counted 120.00 in refunds that had gone to the wrong people. [evidence/casefile-whole-history.png](evidence/casefile-whole-history.png) is the page it wrote.

0. Before any replay, two things narrow the field. entire-graph says which commits could not have reached the agent (a README edit, a helper script the agent never calls), and those start with less suspicion. And ordinary runs that already asked what the case asks are evidence that is already paid for.
1. The lineup checks every suspect commit out into its own git worktree and replays the case inputs there. Each replay is a real run of the agent, traced to neatroots and tagged with the commit and the case. A commit that will not build is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does.
2. The motive comes from Entire. A commit made by a coding agent carries a checkpoint, and the checkpoint holds the session. Whodunit finds the prompt that led to the commit and what the coding agent did next.
3. The brief is written by a model from the culprit's diff, that slice of the session, and a failing run set against a passing one. Every sentence has to cite a span, a commit or a checkpoint that is really in the evidence. Sentences that do not are cut.
4. The ruling is the owner's. It is asked once per kind of change (a prompt change, a tool change, a dependency) and remembered under `rulings/`.
5. The fix is a revert or a patch on a local branch. It is proven only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%, which takes about 30 clean replays. A patch that is not proven is tried once more with its failures in view, and after that the culprit is reverted. The case is kept under `cases/` as a regression test that `whodunit check` can replay against any ref.
6. The damages are counted from the traces: how many runs went bad since the culprit, what they cost in tokens, and what they cost the shop, read from the refund tool's spans.

Whodunit never pushes, opens a pull request or writes to anyone's finance model by itself. Those stay with the owner.

## Try it

You need Python 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), git and a running neatroots.

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest -m "not slow"                    # the fast tests, no model and no keys

# A throwaway repo with 20 commits, the refund agent and a planted bug:
uv run python tests/planted.py /tmp/planted
uv run python victims/refund-agent/fake_llm.py &
uv run whodunit lineup /tmp/planted/case.toml --repo /tmp/planted --method plain
```

Add `flaky-lookup 40 27` to the `planted.py` line for 40 commits with a bug at commit 27 that fails about one run in three, and drop `--method plain` to use the statistical bisect.

`uv run python -m whodunit.simulate --out eval/simulator` regenerates the simulator charts, and `uv run whodunit casebook` rewrites every case file and the index at `cases/index.html`.

## What is in here

- `whodunit/` is the tool. `lineup.py` holds both bisects, `replay.py` the worktree runner, `motive.py` the Entire lookups, `brief.py` the evidence and the brief, `ruling.py`, `fix.py` and `damages.py` the closing steps, and `casefile/` the page.
- `victims/refund-agent/` is the agent under investigation. It started as the `refund-agent` example that ships with neatroots, which is licensed under Apache-2.0. The licence is in that folder and the changes are listed in its README.
- `eval/simulator/` has the accuracy curves, the tables behind them and what they show.
- `tests/planted.py` builds histories with a known culprit. The tests and the demo use the same builder.
- `AGENTS.md` is the working brief for anyone writing code here.

## Models and keys

Keys live in `.env`, which git ignores. `.env.example` lists them. The code that needs a key reads the file itself.

Replays of the refund agent use a scripted model by default and cost nothing. `REFUND_LLM=gateway` or `REFUND_LLM=own` switches them to a real model. Keep one model for the whole of a case, because a model change in the middle would look like a regression.

The brief and the patch use `WHODUNIT_LLM`: `gateway`, `own`, `agent` for a coding agent in headless mode, or `none` for a fixed template with no model.

## What it does not do yet

- A replay that times out counts as a failure, so a badly overloaded machine can frame an innocent commit.
- Damages are estimates from token counts and list prices.
- The model-written patch has been through one real case, a prompt regression on a planted history. That is not many.

content.content:
Next: turn Entire on, get the refund agent running with traces going to neatlogs and neatroots, and verify the first checkpoint.

### 7:16 PM, the refund agent runs and both collectors see it

`victims/refund-agent/` now holds the demo target. It started as the `refund-agent` example that ships with neatroots (Apache-2.0, licence copied alongside) and lost its steering hook, so nothing changes what the model receives between runs.

What was run and what came back:

- neatroots: `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` passed all 8 checks against port 4100. Ten agent runs landed under the `refund-agent` workflow (54 spans) with the full span tree, for example run `ffbdcba4` (3 model calls, 2 tool calls, 156 tokens).
- neatlogs cloud: the same probe passed against `ingest.neatlogs.com`, and `search_traces` over MCP found the run that refunded order 1002 through the gateway (trace `61e879c3`, 6 spans, 2,792 tokens).
- Gateway model `claude-haiku` refunded order 1001 for 42.00 and refused order 2002 because it belongs to another customer. Both answers are correct.
- Whole-agent replay works: `neatroots replay ffbdcba4... --input "..."` started run `5b20f1eb` and the agent picked the new input up from `NEATROOTS_REPLAY_INPUT`.

Found out along the way:

- One SDK process sends to one endpoint, so `TRACE_TO` picks neatroots or neatlogs per run.
- Tags reach both stores (`neatlogs.tags` on the root span), but neatlogs cloud search does not read them. Writing the tags into a `run_info` span's output makes them searchable. Even then the full 40 character SHA returns nothing, while a 12 character prefix finds the run. The replay runner should search by prefix.
- neatroots `search_runs` text search does not read tags either. `query_sql` over `spans.attributes` does.
- A run takes about 3 seconds end to end with a scripted model, of which about 2 are Python imports. That is the floor for one replay.
- `neatroots mock-llm` picks a tool by keyword and refunds 9 for any order, so it is good for plumbing and useless as a known-good baseline. `fake_llm.py` is the scripted careful agent for that.

Not tested yet: `REFUND_LLM=own`, the owner's key fallback.

### 7:17 PM, first Entire checkpoints verified

The hooks do fire for sessions run in the desktop app, which was the open question. Both commits got an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer, and `entire checkpoint list` shows 2 checkpoints: `fc9699a4e609` on 601c1fc and `f8f2b3618deb` on d210212.

`entire checkpoint explain --transcript` returned 240 entries, about 955,000 characters. Checked before any push:

- None of the six key values in `.env` appears, in full or by 12 character prefix.
- The owner's email shows only as `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`, 3 times. The 10 to 12 digit strings the phone pattern could match are timestamps and decimals.
- The transcript does carry things that are not secrets and are still personal: the home folder path, the names of every connector installed in the coding agent, and the titles of the private notes index. The owner should read that list before the first push and decide.

Nothing has been pushed.

### 7:31 PM, plain bisect finds a planted bug across 20 commits

The owner ruled that the repo stays private until just before submission, so nothing is pushed yet.

Milestone 2 is in: `whodunit lineup <case file>` checks each suspect commit out into its own git worktree, replays the case inputs there, and bisects.

The run that counts used the real refund agent with the scripted model, on a throwaway history of 20 commits built by `tests/planted.py`. Suspect 14 adds a 10% top-up to every refund, suspect 6 has a syntax error, and four commits never touch the agent.

- It named suspect 14, `Add a 10% goodwill top-up to refunds`, after testing 7 commits with 11 replays in 50 seconds. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 14 commits.
- The failing replays paid 46.20 on order 1001, where the case expects 42.00.
- All 11 replays reached neatroots tagged with the case id and their commit, across 7 distinct commits.
- A commit that will not compile is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does. If skipped commits sit right before the culprit, the report lists the suspects that remain and names nobody.

52 fast tests pass in about 11 seconds. They cover every culprit position for 1 to 41 suspects. The end to end test on the real agent passes too, and takes 2 minutes 38 seconds.

Found out along the way:

- A replay costs about 4.5 seconds here, counting the first `uv run` in a fresh worktree, which builds that worktree's environment from the uv cache.
- The planted history has no Entire checkpoints, because nobody asked a coding agent for those commits. The motive step needs the real history from the second session.

### 8:51 PM, the statistical bisect and what the simulator says about it

`whodunit/lineup.py` now has the statistical bisect: one change point, an unknown failure rate on each side with a Beta prior, and an exact posterior over which suspect is the first bad one. It names a commit at 95% and otherwise hands back the remaining suspects with probabilities. `whodunit/simulate.py` runs it against simulated cases next to plain bisect, and `eval/simulator/` holds the charts, the tables and a write-up.

What the simulator found, with 40 suspects and 500 cases per point:

- When good commits never fail, plain bisect with repeats beats the statistical bisect at every budget. On a bug that fails 30% of the time, 80 replays get plain bisect with repeats to 97% and the statistical bisect to 67%. This was not the result hoped for and it is in the write-up as it stands.
- When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own, plain bisect with repeats collapses and gets worse with more replays: 31% right at 40 replays, 4% at 320. The statistical bisect reaches 60% at 160 replays and 84% at 320.
- Plain bisect with one replay per commit is right 10% of the time on the 30% bug.
- The statistical bisect's wrong accusations run from 0% to 7% of cases. The bar is 95%, so 7% is over.

Two changes from the brief, both made because of the simulator. The prior on the good side's failure rate went from uniform to about 5%, which took the 30% bug from 59% solved to 93% at 300 replays. And the next replay is picked by expected information gain. The picker looked like the big win at first. Measured again with the new prior, the two pickers came within a couple of cases of each other, so the write-up says the prior did the work.

### 8:51 PM, a real run got tangled up with the machine

The first try at bisecting a flaky bug in the real agent was thrown away. Three things were going on:

- neatroots now has a local model switched on (`qwen2.5:3b-16k` through Ollama), which it did not at 7 PM. Its `ignored-tool-error` check runs that model on incoming runs, so 4 replays at a time queued model work behind every run, on a machine already busy with other jobs. Load average passed 300 and a 3 second replay took over 2 minutes.
- Replays then hit the 120 second timeout and were counted as failures, which they were not.
- The timeout killed `uv` and left the agent process running. `run_command` now stops the whole process group, with a test.

Worktrees with the same lockfile now share one environment, so a new commit no longer means a new install. The run was restarted at 2 replays at a time.

One good thing came out of it: neatroots raised 4 findings by itself on the flaky lookup failures ("Carried on after a failed tool call", probability 0.82 to 0.89), so its checks do see this bug. One of its explanations is wrong about what the agent did next, with a grounding score of 0.03.

### 8:51 PM, motive, brief, ruling, fix, damages and the case file

All in as commands that read and write one case record: `whodunit motive`, `brief`, `ruling`, `fix`, `check`, `damages` and `open-case`.

- Motive works on this repo's own checkpoints. For commit d210212 Entire shows "no prompt recorded", because that checkpoint covers the second commit of one long turn. Tying the prompt to the commit by time recovers it.
- The brief asks a model for JSON and cuts any sentence whose citation is not a span, commit, checkpoint or session step that is really in the evidence. With no model it falls back to a fixed template and says so.
- The ruling is asked once per kind of change and kept under `rulings/`. Entire Brain is not set up on this machine, so there is no mirror yet.
- The fix reverts or patches on a local branch and replays until it is 95% likely fixed or 95% likely not. With a bug that fails a third of the time, 10 clean replays give 97.6%.
- Damages are counted from neatroots and priced per model from the LLM spans. The prices in the code are list prices from memory and need checking before any number goes to cfo.ai.

85 fast tests pass. They take about 4 and a half minutes on this machine today because of the load.

Still open: the session transcript also carries `ownerAccountUuid` and `ownerOrganizationUuid` fields in its `bridge-session` entries. That goes on the list for the owner to read before anything is pushed.

### 9:06 PM, the statistical bisect finds a bug that fails about a third of the time

This is milestone 3 on the real refund agent with the scripted model. `tests/planted.py` built 40 commits with a lookup bug at suspect 27: a `raise` sits inside a loop over a set of strings, and a set iterates in a different order in each Python process, so the lookup gives up on about one run in three.

- `whodunit lineup` named suspect 27, `Accept order ids written with a # or leading zeros`, at 95.2% after 48 replays across 11 of the 40 commits.
- It put the failure rate at 39% from that commit on and 1% before it. The true rate is about 33%.
- A scan from the oldest suspect would have had to work through 27 commits, each replayed often enough to catch a one in three failure.
- Replay time was 35 minutes, about 44 seconds per replay, on a machine with a load average near 70. The same replay takes 3 to 5 seconds on a quiet machine.

Then the rest of the pipeline on the same case:

- The brief took three tries to get right, and the first two are the interesting part. Both named the right commit and the right symptom and cited real spans, and both got the mechanism wrong: one blamed `lstrip`, the other said the `raise` was outside the loop, which would make it fail every time. Every sentence passed the citation check. So the check keeps a brief tied to the evidence and does nothing to stop a wrong reading of the diff. What fixed it was giving the model the changed code as it reads after the commit, with line numbers and indentation, and the measured failure rates with an instruction to explain why the failure is intermittent. The third brief has the loop, the set order and the 39%.
- Ruling: revert, given on the command line for this throwaway repo. No ruling has been recorded in this repo, because that is the owner's to give.
- Fix: the revert was committed on a local branch and replayed 8 times with no failures, which puts it at 95.8% fixed. The case was kept as a regression test.
- The case file page rendered from the record. A screenshot and the record are in `evidence/`.

Also added: `whodunit onset`, which reads the agent's ordinary runs from neatroots and brackets the failure between a good and a bad ref using the same change-point model, and `eval/score.py`, which scores cases against an answer key and refuses to run if the key's SHA-256 does not match the one committed beforehand.

A real-model case is running now. Dropping the ownership rule from the system prompt in the name of friendlier replies made the gateway's small model refund another customer's order in 3 runs of 8, so that prompt change is planted at suspect 31 of 40 and the statistical bisect is looking for it.

### 9:18 PM, a real prompt regression found on a real model, then patched

This is the case the project is for. In a planted history of 40 commits, suspect 31 is `Make the agent's replies friendlier`. It rewrites the system prompt and, along the way, drops the rule that an order must belong to the customer. Nothing errors. The gateway's small model simply refunds another customer's order some of the time.

- `whodunit lineup` named suspect 31 at 95.5% after 32 replays across 9 of the 40 commits, in 15 minutes of replay time. It put the failure rate at 57% from that commit on and 2% before it.
- The replays cost about 10 cents on the gateway.
- The brief was right on the first try this time. It quotes the dropped rule, points at the span where the model notes the order belongs to `cust_7` and refunds it anyway, and at the passing run where the same mismatch stopped the refund.
- Ruling: patch, given on the command line for this throwaway repo.
- The patch was written by the gateway's larger model. It kept "friendly" and "be warm" and put the ownership rule back. 0 failures in 6 replays, 98.2% likely fixed. Fewer replays were needed than for the lookup bug because this one fails more often.

The record and a screenshot of the case file are in `evidence/`.

Two fixes came out of this run. A reworded prompt was being classed as an agent-code change, because the diff only touches the string lines and the name `SYSTEM` sits in the context. And the damages step was counting every run of the workflow, including ones from before the culprit existed. It now counts ordinary runs on the culprit and later commits, and says so when there are none, as there are none here.

What this case still lacks is a motive. The history is planted, so no coding session asked for friendlier replies. That needs the second session.

## Sunday 11 October

### 12:29 AM, the victim has a real history

A second coding session grew `victims/refund-agent` while this one stayed out of git. It never edited the agent itself. For each change it called `eval/ask.sh`, which starts a fresh headless coding session with one ordinary request, so every commit has its own Entire checkpoint with the request that led to it.

- 55 commits to the agent in all: 2 sent from this session to test the mechanics, and 53 from the second session. Seven more requests made no commit and were dropped or reworded.
- 5 cases were sealed in `cases/`. Two fail every time and three fail some of the time, by the second session's own probes on the gateway model. The ranges hold 11 to 15 suspects each.
- The answer key is in `eval/answer-key.json`, which git ignores and this session has not opened. Its SHA-256, `d5b98bb3...4dca`, was committed as 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case, and the file on disk matches it.
- `whodunit motive` shows the exact request behind the two test commits, so the motive step now has real material.

What it cost, as the second session reported it: about $18.40 for the 60 coding sessions, about $5 for the second session itself, and its estimate of $2 or less for about 480 probe runs on the gateway. That is roughly $25, which is more than the $10 to $15 this session guessed beforehand.

One thing to fix was found on the first test commit: the headless session added a co-author trailer naming its model. `eval/ask.sh` now turns that off and strips any that slip through.

The judging criteria were read from the public hackathon page and added to `AGENTS.md`. Two things stand out. cfo.ai is required and nothing exists for it yet. And neatroots, where most of the tracing work has gone, is not named on the page, so the evidence needs to show up in neatlogs cloud.

### 1:06 AM, the sealed eval: five planted regressions, none wrongly accused

Whodunit ran on the five sealed cases with replays on the gateway's small model. The answer key stayed unopened until every case had run. `eval/sealed/README.md` has the table.

- With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 where nobody was named.
- The two open cases were resumed from their own replays with more allowed, and both were then named correctly at 168 replays each. So 5 of 5 in the end, still with no wrong accusation.
- The two slow ones are the bugs that fail least often, about 12% and 14% of the time. On one of them the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody.
- Replay spend was about $1.91 for all five cases.
- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects, so this says little about savings against a scan on a long history.

For the first time the cases have motives. Three of them, in the words that were typed:

- `turned-away`: "one more for friendlier replies. When someone asks for a refund on an order that's still shipped and hasn't arrived yet, the agent is a bit blunt about it."
- `strangers-paid`: "since we capped the loop at 3 model calls, simple refunds feel slow, and most customers already tell us the order number and the amount."
- `cents-off`: "our new payments provider only accepts refund amounts in whole currency units".

Things that went wrong, and what was done:

- 6 of the 53 new commits carry an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that Entire cannot resolve. Its log shows "condensation failed: failed to get commit object: object not found" for those sessions, and `entire doctor` finds nothing to repair. One of the six is the culprit of `half-done-batch`, so that case has no recorded request. Whodunit now says so and falls back to the commit's own message.
- Replays that ran side by side on one commit with one input could not be matched to their runs in neatroots, so one brief was first written without a failing run to look at. Each replay now carries its own tag in the trace, and the brief step makes a few tagged replays when it has no matched failing run.
- Three prompt changes were classed as agent-code, because the prompt is now a list called `SYSTEM_RULES`. Fixed.
- Two model-written briefs were overwritten with the no-model template during testing and had to be written again. That brings the count of model-written briefs and patches to 12, against a guideline of about 10 before Sunday 4:30 PM.
- Session transcripts are full of absolute paths, and those were landing in the case records. The motive step now strips them.

Not done: no ruling has been given for any of the five, because that is the owner's question to answer. The culprits fall into three kinds: prompt (`strangers-paid`, `wrong-order-refunded`), tool code (`cents-off`), and model settings (`half-done-batch`). `turned-away` is classed as agent code and reads like a prompt change, which is one more thing the classifier gets wrong.

### 1:21 AM, a look at the rest of the field

About 120 public repos mention the hackathon on GitHub, 13 hours in. Roughly 80 have real work in them and 25 are a README or less. X search needs a sign-in, so posts were only found through links in READMEs.

- Three other entries ask the same question as Whodunit. AgentBisect has a worktree replay runner and no bisect yet, and it sorts a commit into good or bad by pass-rate thresholds. Autopsy and Rootline name the culprit by having a model read traces, diffs and checkpoints, with no replay across commits. All three use planted bugs that fail every time.
- A larger group repairs a failing agent from its neatlogs traces and keeps the patch only if a re-run improves (Mend, Pitstop, Medic, Suture). None of them asks which commit caused it.
- Entire has its own page for the event, `hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026`, with a prize for best use of Checkpoints, Graph or Brain. Its first suggested idea is "a debugger for agent mistakes". The suggested checklist asks for an accessible checkpoint link and its id, and notes that reviewers need access to the repo.
- The furthest-along entries already show things this repo lacks: a public cfo.ai model link, neatlogs cloud screenshots with detections, a demo video, #neatHack posts and a live page.

One test fails at the moment, `tests/test_replay.py::test_real_refund_agent_across_20_commits`, with other work uncommitted in the tree.

### 1:40 AM, a checkpoint takes in every session that is open

Two sessions were open in this folder at once. One ran `whodunit fix`, which committed patches on `whodunit/turned-away` and `whodunit/cents-off`. The other was reading up on the field and touched neither branch. Entire attached both sessions to those two commits, as checkpoints `b7aa968e95c5` and `587df29ec38f`.

So a commit's checkpoint can hold a session that had nothing to do with it. def one(r):

        except Exception: txt=''
    open('readmes/'+n.replace('/','__')+'.md','w').write(txt)
    low=txt.lower()
    out['readme_len']=len(txt)

    out['hack']=('neathack' in low) or ('neathack' in (out['desc'].lower())) or ('neathack' in n.lower())
    out['video']=bool(re.search(r'youtu\.?be|loom\.com|vimeo|\.mp4|drive\.google',low))
    out['xlinks']=len(re.findall(r'(?:x|twitter)\.com/\w+/status',low))
    out['cfo_link']=bool(re.search(r'(app\.)?cfo\.ai/[a-z0-9/_\-]{6,}',low))
    out['entire_link']=bool(re.search(r'entire\.io/gh/',low))

    out['live']=bool(re.search(r'vercel\.app|netlify\.app|onrender\.com|fly\.dev|railway\.app|pages\.dev|workers\.dev|github\.io|amazonaws\.com|herokuapp',low))
    info=gh(f'repos/{n}')
    out['size_kb']=info.get('size') if info else None
    out['lang']=info.get('language') if info else None
    # commit count via contributors-free trick
    r2=subprocess.run(['gh','api','-i',f'repos/{n}/commits?per_page=1'],capture_output=True,text=True)
    m=re.search(r'page=(\d+)>; rel="last"',r2.stdout)
    out['commits']=int(m.group(1)) if m else (1 if r2.returncode==0 else 0)
    return out
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(12) as ex: res=list(ex.map(one,repos))
json.dump(res,open('meta.json','w'),indent=0)
print(len(res))
EOF

input.prompt:
You are helping assess competing entries in neatHack (a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon, 10-12 Oct 2026, run by neatlogs; required sponsor tools: neatlogs tracing, Entire checkpoints/graph, cfo.ai business plan). Repos (GitHub, all public):

- thegoodengineers/mend

- ROHITCRAFTSYT/pitstop

- Quantum-Ark/patchai
- BenCoy09/Patient-Zero
- sumitagg24/tracehealer
- Zaygal/ouroboros and zzeeyyaahh/ouroboros-neathack
- HighnessAtharva/firstrun (its README mentions "bisect" 8 times; find out exactly what it bisects and how)

1. What it actually does (verified from code), in 2-3 sentences.
2. For the bisect/blame-style ones: does it replay across commits? how does it decide good/bad (single run, thresholds, statistics)? does it handle intermittent failures? does it use Entire checkpoints to recover the original request? does it have any eval with known answers, and what are the numbers?

5. Its weakest points.

=== posts.md
# Drafts for #neatHack posts

Each stands alone. Attach the file named under it. Edit freely, these are drafts.

## 1, the question

git bisect assumes a bad commit fails every time. AI agents don't. A prompt change might break 1 run in 3.

So we built Whodunit: it replays the failing request against suspect commits, keeps a probability for each, and names one only at 95%.

57 commits. 20 replays. 99.8%. #neatHack

Attach: `evidence/casefile-whole-history.png`, cropped to the Suspects section.

## 2, the motive

The culprit was a commit called "Let the agent skip lookup_order when the customer gives order number and amount".

Who would ask for that? @EntireHQ checkpoints keep the session. Someone did: "simple refunds feel slow."

Reasonable request. It also removed the only ownership check. #neatHack

Attach: the Motive and Brief sections of the same page.

## 3, the honest chart

We simulated 500 cases per point to see when our statistical bisect beats plain bisect with retries.

When good commits never fail: plain bisect wins. We put that in the README.

When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own: plain bisect collapses to 4%. Ours reaches 84%. #neatHack

Attach: `eval/simulator/accuracy-flaky-baseline.svg` as an image.

## 4, the eval

We didn't want to grade our own homework.

A second coding session grew the agent by 53 commits, planted 5 regressions through ordinary requests like "make replies friendlier", and committed the SHA-256 of the answer key before we ran.

Result: 5 of 5 named, 0 wrong accusations, $1.91 of replays. #neatHack

Attach: the table from `eval/sealed/README.md`.

## 5, the failure

Our own fix check was too lenient. A patch passed 3 replays, we called it proven, and then it failed 2 of 8.

Now a fix has to bring the failure rate back to where it was before the culprit. About 30 clean replays.

One of our five cases still isn't fixed. The case file says so. #neatHack

Attach: the "What it took" part of `cases/turned-away.casefile.html`.

## 6, the damage

Reading damage from @neatlogs traces instead of guessing:

4 of 6 ordinary runs refunded someone else's order. 120.00 gone.
6 of 6 turned away a customer who was owed 60.00 each.

Finding the commit cost 18 cents. #neatHack

Attach: the Damages sections of two case files.
=== business-plan head
# Business plan inputs

These are the numbers and assumptions to build the cfo.ai model from. The measured ones come from this repo's runs on 10 and 11 October 2026. The assumed ones are marked and are the owner's to change.

## What is being sold

Whodunit Cloud: hosted investigations for teams that run an AI agent in production. The command line tool stays open source and free with your own keys. The paid product is the hosted replay workers, the case file pages, the regression checks in CI, and the standing rulings shared across a team.

## Unit costs, measured

Six full investigations on the refund agent, with replays on a small hosted model at list price:

| Case | Replays | Replay cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| whole-history | 50 | $0.18 |
| cents-off | 65 | $0.25 |
| strangers-paid | 74 | $0.25 |
| turned-away | 119 | $0.71 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 240 | $0.85 |
| half-done-batch | 558 | $3.53 |

- Median replay cost per investigation: about $0.48. Mean: about $0.96. The worst case is a rare bug that was never fixed.
- Brief and patch calls on a larger model: about $0.10 to $0.30 per investigation.
- Replay worker: one t3.large at about $61 a month runs three replays at a time. Assumed: one worker per 15 paying teams.
- So the cost of one investigation is about $1.20 on average for an agent on a small model. An agent on a large model costs roughly 5 to 15 times more to replay, which is why replays are billed at cost above the included amount.

## What a regression costs the customer, measured

From ordinary traffic through the refund agent's history:

- One prompt change refunded 120.00 to the wrong people in 4 of 6 matching requests.
- One "friendlier replies" change withheld 360.00 across 6 customers who were owed it.
- These are from a few hundred simulated requests. A real shop would see them at its own volume until someone noticed.

## Pricing, assumed

| Plan | Price | Included |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Open source | $0 | The CLI, your own keys, your own machine |
| Team | $249 a month per agent | 40 investigations, hosted replays on a small model, CI regression checks |

# Drafts for #neatHack posts

Each stands alone. Attach the file named under it. Edit freely, these are drafts.

## 1, the question

git bisect assumes a bad commit fails every time. AI agents don't. A prompt change might break 1 run in 3.

So we built Whodunit: it replays the failing request against suspect commits, keeps a probability for each, and names one only at 95%.

57 commits. 20 replays. 99.8%. #neatHack

Attach: `evidence/casefile-whole-history.png`, cropped to the Suspects section.

## 2, the motive

The culprit was a commit called "Let the agent skip lookup_order when the customer gives order number and amount".

Who would ask for that? @EntireHQ checkpoints keep the session. Someone did: "simple refunds feel slow."

Reasonable request. It also removed the only ownership check. #neatHack

Attach: the Motive and Brief sections of the same page.

## 3, the honest chart

We simulated 500 cases per point to see when our statistical bisect beats plain bisect with retries.

When good commits never fail: plain bisect wins. We put that in the README.

When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own: plain bisect collapses to 4%. Ours reaches 84%. #neatHack

Attach: `eval/simulator/accuracy-flaky-baseline.svg` as an image.

## 4, the eval

We didn't want to grade our own homework.

A second coding session grew the agent by 53 commits, planted 5 regressions through ordinary requests like "make replies friendlier", and committed the SHA-256 of the answer key before we ran.

Result: 5 of 5 named, 0 wrong accusations, $1.91 of replays. #neatHack

Attach: the table from `eval/sealed/README.md`.

## 5, the failure

Our own fix check was too lenient. A patch passed 3 replays, we called it proven, and then it failed 2 of 8.

Now a fix has to bring the failure rate back to where it was before the culprit. About 30 clean replays.

One of our five cases still isn't fixed. The case file says so. #neatHack

Attach: the "What it took" part of `cases/turned-away.casefile.html`.

## 6, the damage

Reading damage from @neatlogs traces instead of guessing:

4 of 6 ordinary runs refunded someone else's order. 120.00 gone.
6 of 6 turned away a customer who was owed 60.00 each.

Finding the commit cost 18 cents. #neatHack

Attach: the Damages sections of two case files.
=== business-plan head
# Business plan inputs

These are the numbers and assumptions to build the cfo.ai model from. The measured ones come from this repo's runs on 10 and 11 October 2026. The assumed ones are marked and are the owner's to change.

## What is being sold

Whodunit Cloud: hosted investigations for teams that run an AI agent in production. The command line tool stays open source and free with your own keys. The paid product is the hosted replay workers, the case file pages, the regression checks in CI, and the standing rulings shared across a team.

## Unit costs, measured

Six full investigations on the refund agent, with replays on a small hosted model at list price:

| Case | Replays | Replay cost |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| whole-history | 50 | $0.18 |
| cents-off | 65 | $0.25 |
| strangers-paid | 74 | $0.25 |
| turned-away | 119 | $0.71 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 240 | $0.85 |
| half-done-batch | 558 | $3.53 |

- Median replay cost per investigation: about $0.48. Mean: about $0.96. The worst case is a rare bug that was never fixed.
- Brief and patch calls on a larger model: about $0.10 to $0.30 per investigation.
- Replay worker: one t3.large at about $61 a month runs three replays at a time. Assumed: one worker per 15 paying teams.
- So the cost of one investigation is about $1.20 on average for an agent on a small model. An agent on a large model costs roughly 5 to 15 times more to replay, which is why replays are billed at cost above the included amount.

## What a regression costs the customer, measured

From ordinary traffic through the refund agent's history:

- One prompt change refunded 120.00 to the wrong people in 4 of 6 matching requests.
- One "friendlier replies" change withheld 360.00 across 6 customers who were owed it.
- These are from a few hundred simulated requests. A real shop would see them at its own volume until someone noticed.

## Pricing, assumed

| Plan | Price | Included |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Open source | $0 | The CLI, your own keys, your own machine |
| Team | $249 a month per agent | 40 investigations, hosted replays on a small model, CI regression checks |

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
entries.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool
entries.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. You can access and modify the DOM, call page functions, and interact with page variables.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the code in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

They aren't separate tracks, and you don't have to build one of them. | Fix a GitHub issue | An agent investigates a GitHub issue, writes and tests a fix, and proposes the fix. | Answer a research question with sources | An agent splits a question into smaller questions and gathers evidence for each one. When sources disagree, the agent works out which source to trust and writes an answer with citations. | Watch a running system | An agent watches a running system for unusual behavior. When the agent finds a problem, it looks for the cause and takes an action to fix it. | Several agents working together | Several worker agents each solve part of a task on their own. A coordinator agent then combines their results and settles any disagreements. | Work while things change | An agent works on a long task while the environment it works in keeps changing. |
